case_name: Manmohan Nanda v. United India Assurance Co. Ltd.
chunk_text: The Supreme Court held that the duty of disclosure on the insured is not an absolute rule to repudiate every claim. Once the policy has been renewed and premia accepted without objection, minor symptoms not amounting to active medical conditions cannot be utilized as a blanket ground for repudiation under exclusionary clauses. If underwriters issued the policy without medical examination, the insurer cannot later repudiate on technical grounds.
ratio_decidendi: Insurers cannot routinely repudiate claims based on undisclosed pre-existing conditions if broad health status was on record and underwriters failed to seek clarifications prior to policy inception.

case_name: Sulbha Prakash Motegaonkar v. Life Insurance Corporation of India
chunk_text: Repudiation of an insurance claim is impermissible unless there is an established direct causal nexus between the alleged undisclosed medical condition and the actual cause of hospitalization or death. The suppression of lumbar spondylitis cannot justify repudiation of a claim resulting from ischemic heart disease.
ratio_decidendi: The Nexus Principle: Suppression of a disease that has no direct causal connection to the actual condition necessitating claim treatment does not justify repudiation.

case_name: Biman Krishna Bose v. United India Insurance Co. Ltd.
chunk_text: An insurance company carrying out public functions cannot act arbitrarily or unfairly in repudiating continuous coverage or denying renewal benefits. Continuous renewals establish a legitimate expectation of coverage protection that cannot be curtailed by technical repudiation letters.
ratio_decidendi: Insurers have a quasi-public duty of fairness; they cannot exploit technical exclusion clauses after years of continuous renewals.

case_name: Hari Om Agarwal v. Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd.
chunk_text: Insurance companies cannot unilaterally reduce claim amounts under the guise of reasonable and customary charges or proportionate deductions without providing a scientific, published tariff standard to the policyholder prior to admission.
ratio_decidendi: Proportionate deductions and room rent caps cannot be arbitrarily applied without objective, pre-published schedules of hospital charges.

case_name: National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Nitin Khandelwal
chunk_text: In the case of a violation of procedural conditions of the policy, the insurer ought not to repudiate the claim in toto. Technical or procedural delays that do not prejudice the insurer or involve active fraud must be settled on non-standard basis.
ratio_decidendi: Technical procedural breaches (such as delayed intimation) cannot be used as justification for total claim repudiation when the underlying event is genuine.

case_name: Canara Bank v. United India Insurance Co. Ltd.
chunk_text: The rule of contra proferentem applies strictly to insurance contracts. If there is any ambiguity in an exclusionary clause or policy term, it must be interpreted against the insurer who drafted it and in favor of the insured.
ratio_decidendi: Ambiguous exclusion clauses must be interpreted in favor of the insured policyholder under the doctrine of contra proferentem.

case_name: Om Prakash v. Reliance General Insurance and Anr.
chunk_text: It is common knowledge that on hospitalization or theft, the condition of the claimant is not normal. Rejection of claims purely on technical grounds in a mechanical manner will result in loss of confidence of policyholders in the insurance industry. The condition regarding intimation is not a condition precedent to liability.
ratio_decidendi: A genuine claim cannot be rejected solely due to delay in intimation if satisfactory explanation exists for the delay.

case_name: Gurshinder Singh v. Shriram General Insurance Co. Ltd.
chunk_text: The 3-Judge Bench held that mere delay in intimating the insurance company cannot be a ground to deny a genuine claim when the incident is established by police FIR or hospital records. Substantive rights cannot be defeated by strict procedural terms.
ratio_decidendi: Three-Judge Bench affirms: Substantive insurance rights cannot be wiped out by delay in intimating the insurer if the underlying medical event is proven genuine.

case_name: M/s Jai Prakash Tayal v. United India Insurance Co. Ltd.
chunk_text: The High Court struck down the exclusionary clause denying health insurance claims for genetic disorders as unconstitutional and discriminatory under Article 14 and Article 21. Insurers cannot exclude conditions simply because they have a genetic or hereditary component.
ratio_decidendi: Blanket exclusion clauses disallowing claims for genetic or hereditary disorders violate constitutional guarantees and are legally unenforceable.

case_name: Shiva Kant Jha v. Union of India
chunk_text: In emergency conditions, the patient cannot be expected to choose only an empanelled hospital or navigate cashless formalities. Medical claim cannot be denied merely because the treatment was taken in an emergency at a non-empanelled hospital.
ratio_decidendi: Emergency medical treatment taken at non-empanelled or out-of-network hospitals must be reimbursed; network restrictions cannot bar emergency lifesaving care.

case_name: Shikha Nischal v. National Insurance Co. Ltd.
chunk_text: Section 21(4) of the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 mandates that every insurer shall make provision for medical insurance for treatment of mental illness on the same basis as is available for treatment of physical illness. Any clause excluding mental illness from health coverage is void ab initio.
ratio_decidendi: Exclusion of mental illness or psychiatric conditions from health insurance policies is unlawful under the Mental Healthcare Act 2017.

case_name: D. Srinivas v. SBI Life Insurance Co. Ltd.
chunk_text: Where the insurer retained the premium amount and failed to communicate rejection or request medical examination within a reasonable period, acceptance of the proposal is complete. The insurer cannot repudiate the claim on the demise of the insured alleging no policy was formed.
ratio_decidendi: Inordinate retention of insurance premium without communicating rejection amounts to deemed acceptance; subsequent repudiation is invalid.

case_name: Jacob Punnen and Anr. v. United India Insurance Co. Ltd.
chunk_text: An insurer cannot unilaterally alter the terms of a health policy on renewal by introducing sub-limits or capping on specific ailments (such as angioplasty or organ transplant) without giving express prior written notice to the policyholder explaining the modification.
ratio_decidendi: Insurers cannot introduce new sub-limits or room-rent caps on renewed policies without explicit advance disclosure and policyholder consent.

case_name: Sushil Kumar v. National Insurance Co. Ltd.
chunk_text: The denial of cashless authorization by a Third Party Administrator (TPA) does not amount to a final repudiation of insurance liability. If the insured proceeds with treatment and incurs genuine hospitalization expenses, the insurer must process reimbursement on merits.
ratio_decidendi: Denial of cashless facility by TPA is an administrative step and does not preclude policyholder from receiving 100% reimbursement on substantive claim filing.

case_name: Bajaj Allianz General Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Rajendra Singh
chunk_text: An insurance company's in-house medical desk cannot sit in appeal over the clinical decision of the treating doctor on whether active inpatient admission was necessary. If the registered medical practitioner advised admission, the insurer cannot deny claim as outpatient treatment.
ratio_decidendi: The clinical discretion of the treating physician regarding medical necessity of admission cannot be second-guessed or overridden by an insurer's desk auditor.

case_name: Sonell Clocks and Gifts Ltd. v. New India Assurance Co. Ltd.
chunk_text: An insurance company is bound by the specific grounds stated in its repudiation letter. It cannot improve upon its case during consumer litigation or Ombudsman hearings by introducing new, unmentioned exclusion clauses after the fact.
ratio_decidendi: Insurers are strictly barred from inventing new grounds of repudiation during appeal proceedings that were absent in the original repudiation letter.

case_name: New India Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Pushpa Vyas
chunk_text: Hypertension and diabetes are common lifestyle conditions prevalent in modern society and manageable with routine medication. Unless there is evidence of active organ damage or critical hospitalization immediately prior to taking the policy, minor managed blood pressure cannot be treated as concealment of material disease.
ratio_decidendi: Routine, well-managed lifestyle conditions (hypertension/diabetes) do not constitute fraudulent concealment of disease unless directly linked to acute organ damage.

case_name: Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Sanjeev Bagla
chunk_text: Where the insurer delays claim settlement beyond statutory timelines without justified cause, it is liable to pay interest at 2% above the bank rate under IRDAI regulations. Policyholders cannot be starved of legitimate compensation through procedural delays.
ratio_decidendi: Unjustified delay in claim settlement obligates the insurer to pay statutory penal interest over and above the principal claim amount.
